intro.html: Sadness has as many shades as happiness. Some sadness is a passing disappointment (crestfallen); some is a deep, lasting mood (melancholy); some is hopeless (despondent) or lonely (forlorn), and some mixes sorrow with sweetness (wistful, poignant). Choosing the right one tells a reader exactly how a character feels.

Moods: melancholy (deep sadness, a noun), somber (dark and serious), morose (sullen and gloomy), lugubrious (over-the-top mournful). After a loss: despondent (no hope), forlorn (lonely, abandoned), crestfallen (disappointed), disconsolate (beyond comfort). Tender sadness: wistful (longing), poignant (deeply moving).

words.ex: A gentle {melancholy} settled over the house after the last guests drove away.
words.ctx: The song’s cheerful tune hid a deep {melancholy}: its words told of a sailor who never came home.
words.etym: From Greek melankholia, “black bile”: doctors long ago blamed lasting sadness on too much black bile in the body.
words.note: Melancholy is also an adjective: a melancholy song.

mn.text: Ever since his melon ball rolled into the river, the old collie lies by the window and sighs all day. Poor melon-collie: he is full of {melancholy}.

scene.alt: A sad old dog lies by the window beside a melon, sighing.

words.ex: The {somber} gray sky matched our mood on the last day of vacation.
words.ctx: The usually noisy classroom was {somber} that morning; the students spoke in low voices after hearing that their favorite teacher was moving away.

mn.text: Clouds bar the sun, the sky turns gray, and the picnic goes quiet and serious. With the sun barred, the mood is {somber}.

scene.alt: Two people stand quietly at a gray picnic as clouds cover the sun.

words.def: in low spirits from loss of hope
words.ex: After the third rejection letter, Felix was {despondent}.
words.ctx: The team was {despondent} after losing the final by a single point, and for days afterward no one could bear to talk about the game.
words.etym: From Latin despondere, “to give up, to lose heart”: de (away) + spondere (to promise).

mn.cue: de-SPOND-ent: no hope by the POND
mn.text: Felix has fished the pond all day without a single nibble, and now he slumps on the bank, all hope gone. He is {despondent}.

scene.alt: A man slumps on a pond bank after catching nothing, while a fish leaps behind him.

words.ex: A {forlorn} teddy bear sat in the rain beside the empty swing.
words.ctx: After the carnival packed up and drove away, the field looked {forlorn}: just trampled grass, a torn ticket and one lonely balloon caught in a fence.

mn.text: Everyone has gone home from the playground, and one little teddy bear sits all alone on the bench in the rain. It looks {forlorn}.

scene.alt: A lonely teddy bear sits on an empty playground bench in the rain.

words.ex: The {morose} goalie barely spoke during the long bus ride home.
words.ctx: Usually cheerful, Uncle Marcus turned {morose} whenever it rained: he sat in his armchair, scowling, and answered every question with a grunt.
words.etym: From Latin morosus, “peevish, hard to please.”

mn.cue: MO-ROSE: no ROSE can cheer him
mn.text: Lin brings Marcus a rose to cheer him up, and he only scowls and grunts. No rose can brighten his sullen mood: he is {morose}.

scene.alt: A scowling man under a little rain cloud ignores the rose a woman offers him.

words.def: deeply moving; stirring sadness or tender regret
words.ex: Grandpa’s {poignant} letter to his younger self made the whole family cry.
words.ctx: The film’s last scene was {poignant}: the two friends, now old men, met again at the very station where they had said goodbye sixty years before.
words.etym: From Old French poignant, “pricking,” from Latin pungere, “to prick,” the root of pungent.
words.note: Say POIN-yunt: the g is silent.

mn.cue: POIGN-ant: POINTS straight at the heart
mn.text: Two old friends meet again on the platform where they said goodbye sixty years before, and the moment points straight at your heart. It is {poignant}.

scene.alt: Two old friends hug and cry on a station platform after sixty years apart.

words.ex: Kai was {crestfallen} when the trip to the lake was canceled.
words.ctx: Sami had practiced his speech for weeks, so he was {crestfallen} when the assembly was called off at the last minute.

roots.means: the comb or plume on top of the head

words.etym: From crest, the comb on a bird’s head or the plume on a helmet, + fallen: the word pictures a drooping crest.

mn.text: Rocky the rooster loses the crowing contest, and his proud red comb flops down over one eye. He is {crestfallen}.

scene.alt: A sad rooster droops after losing, while the winning rooster stands proudly by a trophy.

words.def: so sad that nothing can comfort
words.ex: The {disconsolate} toddler cried for an hour after his balloon floated away.
words.ctx: Friends brought cards, cookies and funny movies, but Ivy remained {disconsolate}; nothing could make up for her best friend moving across the country.

mn.text: Theo’s balloon floats away, and nothing helps: not a hug, not a cookie, not even a new balloon. He cannot be consoled; he is {disconsolate}.

scene.alt: A toddler cries as his balloon floats away; his grandmother’s cookie does not help.

words.def: sadly longing for something past or out of reach
words.ex: Grandma gave a {wistful} smile as she looked through her old dance photos.
words.ctx: Watching his friends ride off to summer camp, Pip grew {wistful}; he had loved camp, but this year his family could not afford to send him.

mn.text: Granny Mae turns the pages of her old dance photos, smiling but a little sad, wishing she could dance like that once more. Her smile is {wistful}.

scene.alt: A grandmother smiles a little sadly as she looks through an old photo album.

words.def: mournful, often in an exaggerated way
words.ex: The hound gave a {lugubrious} howl whenever the family left the house.
words.ctx: The actor played the old butler in a {lugubrious} voice so slow and gloomy that the audience, instead of crying, burst out laughing.
words.etym: From Latin lugubris, “mournful,” from lugere, “to mourn.”

mn.cue: lu-GOO-brious: a howl as slow as GOO
mn.text: Every time the car pulls away, Biscuit the hound lets out a howl as slow and droopy as goo: “Aroooooo.” It is over the top, and it is {lugubrious}.

scene.alt: A droopy dog howls mournfully as the family car drives away.

head: word
the kind of sadness
rows: moving: sad and tender at once
after.cap: Shades of sadness, from a moment to a mood.

after.html: poignant is said POIN-yunt (the g is silent), and it can describe a tender, happy-sad memory, not only a sad one. morose adds bad temper to gloom; a morose person is sulking, not just sad.

items.q: Which word describes someone gloomy and grumpy?
items.why: Morose means sullen and bad-tempered as well as gloomy.

items.q: Looking at photos of the beach house they used to rent, Dad sighed. He was feeling…
items.why: A gentle, sad longing for something in the past is wistful.

items.q: True or false: the g in poignant is silent.

choices: a drooping crest, like a rooster’s comb
a mountain whose top has crumbled
a knight falling off his horse
items.why: A crest is the comb or plume on top of the head; crestfallen pictures it drooping. The word means disappointed and downcast.
